Learning Objectives
Assess the anatomy of the foot and ankle, including the hindfoot, midfoot, and forefoot, and
their complex interplay.
Determine the foot and ankle locomotor and gait cycles.
Analyze the critical effect of the tarsal joint locking mechanism resulting from static and
dynamic interplay, leading to normal and pathologic functions with impaired motion coupling.
Implement the basic understanding of the foot as a tripod with alteration of anatomic force
imbalances that lead to substantial malalignment and biomechanical consequences.
Measure alteration of normal gait and identify how it may result in specific gait dysfunction
and implications in clinical presentation.

Overview
The field of foot and ankle biomechanics has substantially expanded over the past few years,
leading to better understanding of the basics of foot and ankle anatomy, function, and
biomechanics, as well as the effects of ankle/foot malalignment leading to altered gait and
impaired function.
Vascular Anatomy
Arteries
Three major arteries typically supply the ankle and foot.
Posterior tibial artery—This artery bifurcates into the medial and lateral plantar arteries
beneath the sustentaculum.
Peroneal artery—The peroneal artery arises from the tibioperoneal trunk and forms a
perforating artery that pierces the interosseous membrane at the distal third of the leg.
Anterior tibial artery—This artery arises from the popliteal artery below the knee and
descends through the anterior compartment of the leg. It combines variably with the
perforating branch of the peroneal artery to form the dorsalis pedis artery.
Plantar arcades—The medial plantar artery and lateral plantar artery typically include
superficial and deep branches, which undergo anastomosis distally in the midfoot to supply
the superficial plantar arcade and deep plantar arch.
Osseous vascular supply of interest
Talus (Figure 1)
60% of the talar surface is covered with articular cartilage, limiting the potential sites for
arterial supply to five bony regions: the tarsal canal, sinus tarsi, superior neck, medial body,
and posterior tubercle.
Injection studies have demonstrated that the talar neck is well vascularized by an
anastomotic ring of vessels that receives blood dorsally from the dorsalis pedis artery,
laterally from the perforating peroneal artery through the lateral tarsal artery, and
inferiorly through the artery of the tarsal canal.
The talar body receives most of its blood supply retrograde through the artery of the tarsal
canal, which predisposes it to osteonecrosis and nonunion after talar neck fractures and
talar dislocations.

The navicular is prone to stress fracture in the dorsal third, the location at which

Fifth metatarsal
Penetrating the fifth metatarsal medially at the junction of its proximal and middle thirds,
the main nutrient vessel to the fifth metatarsal then divides into proximal and distal
vessels.
The proximal blood supply to the fifth metatarsal is through the tuberosity, creating a
watershed area at the proximal metaphyseal/diaphyseal junction, which is prone to stress
fractures and nonunion.

Tibial nerve—The tibial nerve travels in the deep posterior compartment of the leg and has
three major branches.
Medial calcaneal nerve—This nerve innervates the plantar medial heel.
Medial plantar nerve—This nerve supplies sensory innervation to the plantar medial foot; the
plantar aspect of the first, second, and third toes; and the medial half of the fourth toe. It
provides motor innervation to the flexor hallucis brevis, abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum
brevis, and the first lumbrical.
Lateral plantar nerve—This nerve provides sensation to the plantar lateral foot, the lateral
fourth toe, and the fifth toe. Motor innervation is provided to the remaining plantar muscles
not innervated by the medial plantar nerve.

The first branch of the lateral plantar nerve (Baxter nerve) courses anterior to the medial
calcaneal tuberosity between the quadratus plantae and the flexor digitorum brevis,
terminally innervating the abductor digiti minimi.
The Baxter nerve is implicated in heel pain but provides no cutaneous innervation.
Superficial peroneal nerve—The superficial peroneal nerve divides into medial and
intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerves of the foot proximal to the ankle.
Deep peroneal nerve (DPN)—The DPN travels in the anterior compartment, where it
innervates the tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, and extensor hallucis longus (EHL),
and courses between the tibialis anterior and EHL tendons. It innervates the extensor
digitorum brevis and the extensor hallucis brevis muscles in the foot and provides sensation to
the first dorsal web space.
Sural nerve—The sural nerve has a variable origin from confluent branches of the tibial and
common peroneal nerves. It provides sensation to the dorsolateral foot and dorsal fourth and
fifth toes.
Saphenous nerve—The saphenous nerve is the terminal branch of the femoral nerve and
supplies sensation to the medial side of the foot.
Joints and Ligaments
Bones and ligaments
The ankle joint (Figure 3)
The ankle joint includes the tibia, talus, and fibula.
It is a ginglymus (hinge) joint.
The talar dome is biconcave with a central talar sulcus.
The radius of curvature is greater laterally.
Viewed axially, the joint is trapezoidal and wider anteriorly than posteriorly.
The talus is the only tarsal bone without muscular or ligamentous insertions.
The medial malleolus and lateral malleolus have osseous grooves for the posterior tibial
tendon (PTT) and the peroneal tendons, respectively.
Lateral ankle ligaments—The lateral ankle ligamentous complex is composed of three
ligaments:
Anterior talofibular ligament—The anterior talofibular ligament extends from the anterior
aspect of the distal fibula to the body of the talus. Strain in this ligament increases with
plantar flexion, inversion, and internal rotation.

Calcaneofibular ligament—The calcaneofibular ligament extends from the tip of the fibula
posterior to its insertion on the lateral wall of the calcaneus. It runs deep to the peroneal
tendons and crosses the subtalar joint. This ligament is under increased strain with
dorsiflexion and inversion.
Posterior talofibular ligament—The posterior talofibular ligament originates broadly at
the posterior fibula and inserts mainly at the posterolateral tubercle of the talus. It is a
broad, strong ligament that is congruous with the posterior capsule of the ankle and
subtalar joint.
Deltoid ligament
The deltoid ligament is a triangle-shaped ligament with the apex at the medial malleolus
and with fibers extending to the calcaneus, talus, and navicular.
The ligament is divided into superficial and deep components. The superficial component
has three parts, extending anteriorly to the navicular, inferiorly to the sustentaculum, and
posteriorly on the talar body. The deep deltoid ligament extends in two bands from the
medial malleolus to the talar body just inferior to the medial facet.
Syndesmosis—The tibiofibular articulation is composed of the tibial incisura fibularis and
its corresponding fibular facet. It has three ligamentous structures that are variably
responsible for its support: the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (35%), interosseous
ligament (22%), and posterior talofibular ligament (43%).

Figure 3 Illustrations of an ankle show the subtalar ligaments viewed laterally (A) and anteriorly
(B). (Reproduced from Katcherian D: Soft-tissue injuries of the ankle, in Lutter LD, Mizel MS,
Pfeffer GB, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Foot and Ankle. Rosemont, IL, American Academy
of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 1994, pp 241-253.)
Hindfoot and midfoot
The subtalar joint has three facets: one posterior, one in the middle, and one anterior.
The posterior facet is the largest.
The middle facet rests on the sustentaculum of the calcaneus and is located medially.
The anterior facet often is continuous with the talonavicular joint.
The transverse tarsal joint (Chopart joint) is composed of the talonavicular and
calcaneocuboid joints and acts in concert with the subtalar joint to control foot flexibility
during gait.
The talonavicular joint is supported by the spring ligament complex, which has two
separate components: the superior medial calcaneonavicular ligament and the inferior
calcaneonavicular ligament
The calcaneocuboid joint is saddle-shaped. It is supported plantarly by the inferior
calcaneocuboid ligaments (superficial and deep) and superiorly by the lateral limb of the
bifurcate ligament.
The naviculocuneiform and intercuneiform joints are connected by dense ligamentous
structures that allow little motion between the joints.
The tarsometatarsal (TMT) joint consists of the first, second, and third
metatarsocuneiform joints and the fourth and fifth metatarsocuboid joints.
The osseous anatomy functions as a transverse Roman arch in the axial plane, with the
dorsal surface wider than the plantar surface.
The second metatarsal base functions as the keystone.
The ligamentous support of the TMT joint has three layers. The strongest layer is the
interosseous layer, which includes the Lisfranc ligament (Figure 4). This ligament
originates from the plantar aspect of the medial cuneiform and extends to the base of
the second metatarsal. The plantar layer is the next strongest, and the dorsal layer is the
weakest.

The anterior compartment contains the tibialis anterior, EHL, extensor digitorum longus, and
peroneus tertius muscles, as well as the anterior tibial artery and the DPN. Deep to the

The superficial posterior compartment contains the gastrocnemius-soleus complex and the
plantaris muscle.

Two heads of the gastrocnemius muscle originate from the medial and lateral femoral
condyles and act as knee flexors and ankle plantar flexors.
The soleus originates on the tibia and fibula. It runs deep to the gastrocnemius and joins it
distally to form the Achilles tendon.
The Achilles tendon fibers twist medially 90° so the superficial fibers at the myotendinous
junction insert laterally on the calcaneus.
The plantaris is absent in 7% of individuals.
The deep posterior compartment contains the PTT, flexor digitorum longus (FDL), and flexor
hallucis longus (FHL), which become entirely tendinous as they enter the ankle.
Posterior to the medial malleolus, the posterior compartment structures enter the fibro-
osseous tarsal tunnel.
Oriented from anteromedial to posterolateral in the tarsal tunnel are the PTT, FDL tendon,
posterior tibial artery, tibial nerve, and FHL tendon.
The FHL and FDL have interconnections at the knot of Henry in the plantar midfoot.
The lateral compartment contains the peroneus longus and peroneus brevis muscles, the
superficial peroneal nerve, and the peroneal artery.
The tendons enter a system of fibro-osseous tunnels posterior to the fibula to the level of
their insertion.
The superior peroneal retinaculum is located at the distal 3 cm of the fibula; the inferior
peroneal retinaculum is contiguous with the inferior extensor retinaculum dorsally and
inserts on the peroneal tubercle of the calcaneus, which divides the peroneal tendon
sheath into separate compartments for the peroneus brevis (dorsal) and the peroneus
longus (plantar).
The peroneus brevis inserts at the base of the fifth metatarsal.
The peroneus longus curves sharply beneath the cuboid, at which it crosses plantarly to
insert medially at the base of the first TMT joint. An osseous groove is present at the
plantar cuboid, and an os peroneum is present in 5% to 26% of individuals.
Accessory peroneals (including the peroneus quartus) are present in 12% of individuals and
can contribute to pathology (Figure 7).

Muscles of the plantar foot
First layer—The first layer is the most superficial of the plantar layers. It contains the flexor
digitorum brevis, abductor hallucis, and abductor digiti minimi muscles.
Second layer—This layer contains the quadratus plantae and lumbrical muscles and the FDL
and FHL tendons. On the plantar surface of this layer lie the medial and lateral plantar
arteries and nerves.
Third layer—The third layer contains the oblique and transverse heads of the adductor
hallucis, flexor hallucis brevis, and flexor digiti minimi brevis muscles.
Fourth layer—This layer is the deepest. It contains the fibro-osseous tunnels along which the
posterior tibial and peroneus longus tendons travel to their final insertions. It contains the

four dorsal interossei, three plantar interossei, and four lumbrical muscles.
Muscles of the dorsal foot
Laterally, the extensor digitorum brevis arises from the anterior process of the calcaneus.
Medially, the extensor hallucis brevis is variably present.
Each of these muscles contributes tendinous slips to the long extensor tendons or directly to
the base of each proximal phalanx.
Deep to these muscles course the dorsalis pedis artery and the DPN.
Biomechanics
Ankle and syndesmosis
The ankle joint consists of the tibia, fibula, and talus.
Its primary motion is dorsiflexion and plantar flexion.
With the foot fixed, dorsiflexion is accompanied by internal tibial rotation, and plantar
flexion is accompanied by external tibial rotation.
The bimalleolar axis runs obliquely at 82° (±4°) in the coronal plane and defines the main
motion of the ankle.
The talus is wider anteriorly than posteriorly, and the contact area of the dome of the talus
increases and moves anteriorly with dorsiflexion.
Increased load transmission in the malleoli also occurs with dorsiflexion.
The fibula transmits approximately 10% to 15% of the axial load.
The tibiofibular syndesmosis allows rotation and proximal and distal migration of the fibula
with the tibia but little motion in the sagittal or coronal planes.
Hindfoot—Subtalar joint and transverse tarsal (Chopart) joint
These joints act through a series of coupled motions to create inversion and eversion of the
hindfoot and to lock and unlock the midfoot.
The transverse tarsal joint consists of the talonavicular and calcaneocuboid articulations.
Inversion of the subtalar joint locks the transverse tarsal joint; eversion unlocks the joint
(Figure 8).

Figure 8 Illustrations show inversion (A) and eversion (B) of the subtalar joint, which locks
and unlocks the transverse tarsal joint by aligning or deviating the major joint axes of the
talonavicular (TN) and calcaneocuboid (CC) joints. (Adapted with permission from Mann RA,
Haskell A: Biomechanics of the foot and ankle, in Coughlin MJ, Mann RA, Saltzman CL, eds:
Surgery of the Foot and Ankle, ed 8. Philadelphia, PA, Mosby, 2007, p 21.)
The joints are parallel during heel strike, with the calcaneus in eversion, allowing the midfoot
to be flexible for shock absorption as the foot accepts the body’s weight.
The joint axes are deviated as the subtalar joint moves to inversion (eg, during push-off),
making the foot inflexible so that it provides a rigid lever arm for push-off.
The relationships of the tendons as they cross the ankle and subtalar joints are shown in
Figure 9.

Figure 9 Illustration superimposed on an MRI of an ankle shows the relationships of the
tendons that cross the ankle joint to the axes of the subtalar and tibiotalar articulations.
Tendons anterior to the ankle axis create a dorsiflexion moment, whereas tendons posterior
to the ankle axis create a plantar flexion moment. Tendons medial to the subtalar axis cause
inversion, whereas tendons lateral to the subtalar axis cause eversion. (Reproduced from
Sammarco VJ, Taylor R: Anatomy and biomechanics of the foot and ankle, in Lieberman JR,
ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1113-1124.)
TMT and midfoot joints
Little motion occurs through the intercuneiform and naviculocuneiform joints.
The fourth and fifth TMT joints are the most mobile, with a range of motion of 5° to 17°. The

Walking is characterized by a period of double limb support, during which both feet are in
contact with ground. Conversely, running is characterized by a period during which both feet
are off the ground with an absence of double limb support.
Normal human gait is highly coordinated, with concerns focused in energy and oxygen

foot.
Cadence is defined by the number of steps taken during a given unit of time.

In walking, a single stride is divided into two major phases: stance (60%) and swing (40%).
Stance is subdivided into heel strike, midstance, and push-off.
There are three intervals of the stance phase:
Interval 1—Heel strike to foot flat, which is weight acceptance and rapid ankle plantar flexion
(controlled by eccentric contraction of the anterior compartment musculature)
Interval 2—Foot flat past midstance; the center of gravity is passing over the fixed planted
foot. Progressive ankle dorsiflexion is controlled by eccentric posterior muscle contracture.
Interval 3—Further progression to toe-off; the ankle rapidly plantarflexes by concentric
contracture of posterior compartment muscles. The hindfoot is locked in varus for push-off.
The swing phase, which consists of the remaining 40% of the gait cycle, extends from toe-off
until the heel strikes the ground. This represents a period in which the limb advances forward
and is not in contact with the ground.

inward deviation of the foot and dorsiflexion results in outward deviation (Figure 12).

Bone and Joint Position
Eversion and inversion of the subtalar joint are directly related to internal and external
rotation of the tibia. Walking is similar to a controlled fall, so as the tibia internally
rotates, the talus begins to evert, and the calcaneus begins to invert. External rotation of
the tibia results in inversion of the talus, and the calcaneus begins to evert. The
relationship must be normal to have a normal gait. Alteration of the joint dynamics may
result in loss of range of motion, leading to an abnormal gait until that motion is
restored.

To obtain a rigid forefoot with the foot fixed to the ground (ie, push-off phase), the
transverse tarsal joint supinates. Conversely, on heel strike, the transverse tarsal joint
becomes flexible in pronation. Coupled motion between the ankle and subtalar joints
consists of the first interval—tibia internally rotates, talus everts, foot pronates, and the
hindfoot is in valgus. In the third interval, the tibia externally rotates, talus inverts, foot
supinates, and the hindfoot is in varus. The MTP break occurs if the heel is elevated; the
weight-bearing forces are evenly distributed across the metatarsal heads.
Muscle Tendon Contraction (Eccentric/Concentric)
Electromyography measurements provide insight into muscle function during the specific
phase of normal gait.
At heel strike, anterior muscles (ie, tibialis anterior) via eccentric action facilitate the descent of
the foot in a controlled manner to absorb ground reaction forces and avoid pathologic
slapping.
Flexors (ie, tibialis posterior) prepare the foot for heel rise via inversion (please see this effect
on transverse tarsal joints) to facilitate push-off.
At single leg stance, the peroneal tendons provide stability to prevent varus alignment as the
ankle rotates in dorsiflexion.
Subsequently, the forces generated by the triceps surae activate, followed by toe flexors to
cause heel rise, and rapid plantar flexion, leading to the toe-off aspect of gait.
Repeating the cycle back into in the swing phase, the plantar flexor muscles will relax, and the
extensor activates for ankle dorsiflexion for clearance of the foot, leading repetition of the
cycle.
Medial Longitudinal Arch and Windlass Mechanism
The medial longitudinal arch aids in shock absorption and accommodation of heel
strike/midstance, leading to efficient propulsion at toe-off.
Two models (beam and truss) have been proposed to describe the biomechanics of medial
longitudinal arch support to provide insight into the medial longitudinal arch and the concept
of the windlass mechanism.
The windlass mechanism is a mechanistic concept that describes the manner in which the
plantar fascia supports the foot during weight-bearing activities.

Pathologic Gait
The key issues of abnormal gait pattern with insufficiencies lie in increased energy usage and
oxygen consumption.
Characteristic patterns of pathologic human gait
Antalgic gait results from pain and is defined by shortened stance phase of the affected limb.
Steppage gait results from footdrop or weakness of anterior or extensor musculature. The
individual is trying to clear the foot during swing phase and this allows the foot to clear.
Calcaneus gait is exaggerated heel weight-bearing and results from weakness or paralysis of
the posterior compartment.
Waddling gait is the result of proximal myopathy and is characterized by broad-based stance,
with the pelvis dropping to the leg being raised during the swing phase.
Trendelenburg gait is caused by weakness of the hip abductor and compensatory lurch of the
trunk to weakened side

Pathologic Gait
Alterations of normal gait lead to insufficiencies that cause increased energy and oxygen
consumption. This concept is emphasized in patients who have undergone an
amputation; the more proximal the amputation, the more required energy expenditure
for ambulation.4
By identifying and managing the underlying cause of the gait disturbance, for example a
patient with ankle arthritis managed with total ankle arthroplasty or ankle arthrodesis,
various parameters of gait can be substantially improved compared with preoperative
function.5 However, even patients who undergo ankle arthrodesis will have residual
effects with shortened stride length, with the potential for persistent deterioration
because of the associated risk of ipsilateral hindfoot arthritis.6

Patients with flatfoot deformity secondary to adult-acquired flatfoot deformity (AAFD),
pes planus, Lisfranc posttraumatic osteoarthritis, or Charcot midfoot arthropathy
commonly report medial arch pain, forefoot abduction, increasing loss of arch height,
and midfoot collapse (Resource 1). Ambulation is extremely difficulty because of
weakness of push-off secondary to the unlocked traverse tarsal joint and inability to
form a rigid foot lever arm for the push-off phase of gait. Gradually, increasing forefoot
abduction with arch collapse, peritalar subluxation, and increased hindfoot valgus
alignment leads to lateral ankle pain with fibular impingement, which may further affect
the transverse tarsal and horizontal subtalar joint, Achilles tendon contracture, and
increasing midfoot-hindfoot arthritis (Resource 2).7-9
The concept of muscle balance is critical in understanding the effect of agonist-
antagonist muscle imbalance of the tibialis anterior versus the peroneus longus (leading
to plantarflexed first ray) and the PTT versus the peroneus brevis (leading to hindfoot
varus with increasing ankle sprain). Pathomechanics of cavovarus foot are understood
by gradual relative loss of muscle function from distal to proximal.10,11
Classically, the clinical presentation of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is an increasing
symmetrical bilateral neurologic impairment starting distally, with loss of function of
intrinsic foot muscles followed by peroneal (specifically peroneus brevis) gradual
weakness propagation to extensor groups (tibialis anterior and long toe extensor) and
lastly to the calf muscles.
Clinical presentation of cavovarus foot initially includes loss of intrinsics with claw toes,
plantar flexed first ray (via overpull by the peroneus longus) with increasing medial shift
of talonavicular/calcaneal cuboid complex (via overpull of the PTT), which locks the
subtalar joint in supination. This deformity leads to cavovarus foot alignment and
increasing hindfoot varus.12 One key issue of ambulation lies in the varus component of
the hindfoot, which leads to loss of stability in the stance phase and tendency for ankle
instability or recurrent ankle sprains. Another problem during ambulation is the
development of early footdrop that occurs with weakness of the tibialis anterior, leading
to long extensor recruitment in an attempt to compensate, especially in the swing phase
of gait, which will exacerbate the claw-toe deformity. Late presentation may include
complete footdrop and a tight Achilles tendon secondary to gastrocsoleus plantar fascia

A clinical correlation that demonstrates these concepts is a FDL transfer with calcaneal
osteotomy for AAFD. The FDL is in phase with PTT harvest, and transfer to the plantar
medial navicular re-creates the moment of the PTT. In addition, the efficiency of the
transferred tendon can improve via medialization of the insertion point. Relative
strength of the FDL is weak (only 30%); therefore, isolated FDL procedures are prone to
fail. A medial displacement calcaneal slide or lateral column lengthening is a useful
adjunct for AAFD.18
This emphasizes another aspect of the effect of anatomic biomechanics. The mild valgus
in a normal hindfoot becomes more pronounced in patients with AAFD. A medial
displacement calcaneal slide translates the insertion of the Achilles tendon/triceps surae
medially (which allows the vector of pull of varus moment at the subtalar joint and pull
closer to the leg mechanical axis); this alteration reduces the antagonistic forces of the
Achilles tendon and decreases medial supporting structure strain, including deltoid and
spring ligament complexes.19,20
Additional support medially is possible by correcting talonavicular lateral subluxation via
spring ligament reefing and/or lateral column lengthening.21
Equinus deformity may lead to peritalar subluxation, midfoot instability, and overload
similar to metatarsalgia. Contracture may be from the gastrocnemius, soleus, or both.
Addressing this contracture often is done at the level of the Achilles tendon. Correctly
identifying the underlying cause of the contracture and providing surgical management
is important to prevent progression of possible deformities. The Silfverskiöld test is used
